s: Holmes (2019) reads Stoic cosmic sympathy as an experiment in 'cosmobiology': it makes a web of interconnected natures, human and non-human, visible as a feature of the world, and has to hold together the integrity of individual natures with the strict unity of a cosmos to which every part is subordinated.

s: Brouwer (2015) objects to treating sympathy as cosmic from the start: the word was first used for the relation between the human body and soul, and the Stoics expanded that relation into a feature of the whole natural world, through the soul pervading all matter.

s: Ancient sympathy was not only a cosmic bond. It sat at three sites at once: in the body (Galen's organ sympathies, explained by nerves; Cicero's dream that passes stones), in the cosmos and its signs (the Stoics' and Posidonius' grounds for divination, Plotinus' one living animal with its magic and perception), and in the relation of soul to gods. Cicero kept the bodily and physical cases and refused the divinatory ones.

s: In the Leitfaden der Psychologie (1903) Lipps makes Einfühlung the source of the third kind of knowledge: things are known by sense perception, the self by inner perception, and other individuals by Einfühlung, defined as feeling a determination of oneself immediately as belonging to the object.

src.l: Theodor Lipps, 1903, Leitfaden der Psychologie
src.loc: ch. XIV 'Die Einfühlung', §'Einfühlung überhaupt' (p. 187 per contents)

src.l: Theodor Lipps, 1903, Leitfaden der Psychologie

s: Lipps also treats our reading of activity and causal dependence into natural things as Einfühlung — the same act of ensouling by which we feel striving into a column — and insists that this Einfühlung is not knowledge and must be strictly separated from what is actually known.

src.l: Theodor Lipps, 1905, Psychologische Untersuchungen, Bd. I
src.loc: Bd. I, discussion of causal relations (archive.org OCR)

s: Jung (Psychologische Typen, 1921) defines Einfühlung as a projection of the subject into the object, resting on an unconscious primary identification (participation mystique): empathizing with a tree means experiencing it as animate.

src.l: C. G. Jung, 1921, Psychologische Typen
src.q: If I empathize with a tree, I project my subjective feeling into the tree and experience it as animate. This projection is an unconscious identification of the subject with the object.
src.qo: Wenn ich mich in einen Baum einfühle, so projiziere ich mein subjektives Gefühl in den Baum und erlebe ihn als beseelt. Diese Projektion ist eine unbewusste Identifizierung des Subjekts mit dem Objekt.

s: Vernon Lee (Beauty & Ugliness, 1912) adopts Titchener's 'Empathy' for aesthetic Einfühlung and calls it analogous to moral sympathy.

src.l: Vernon Lee, C. Anstruther-Thomson, 1912, Beauty & Ugliness and Other Studies in Psychological Aesthetics
src.loc: essay 'Beauty and Ugliness', with footnote citing Titchener 1909 p. 21

s: Southard (1918) borrows Titchener's 'empathy' from aesthetics into psychiatric diagnosis as an 'empathic index', and separates it from sympathy: sympathy is an emotional attitude, empathy an effort of imagination by which we 'read or feel ourselves into' a person, group or nation.

src.l: E. E. Southard, 1918, The empathic index in the diagnosis of mental diseases
E. E. Southard, 1918, The empathic index in the diagnosis of mental diseases

s: Batson et al. (1981) test the empathy-altruism hypothesis: subjects high in empathic emotion helped a shocked victim as readily when escape was easy as when it was difficult, which they read as altruistic rather than egoistic motivation.

src.l: C. Daniel Batson, Bruce D. Duncan, Paula Ackerman, Terese Buckley, Kimberly Birch, 1981, Is empathic emotion a source of altruistic motivation?

s: Hatfield, Cacioppo & Rapson name 'emotional contagion' the phenomenon by which a mood such as elation or depression is communicated from one person to another, and gather evidence for it across psychology, history and psychopathology.

src.l: Elaine Hatfield, John T. Cacioppo, Richard L. Rapson, 1994, Emotional Contagion

s: Preston & de Waal (2002) propose a Perception-Action Model: perceiving an object's state activates the subject's corresponding representations, which activate somatic and autonomic responses; this mechanism is meant to unify emotional, cognitive and conditioning views of empathy across species.

src.l: Stephanie D. Preston, Frans B. M. de Waal, 2002, Empathy: Its ultimate and proximate bases

s: Decety & Jackson (2004) define empathy as felt similarity between one's own and another's feelings without losing track of whose feelings are whose, built from shared neural representations, self-awareness, mental flexibility and emotion regulation.

src.l: Jean Decety, Philip L. Jackson, 2004, The functional architecture of human empathy

s: Lamm, Decety & Singer's meta-analysis (2011; 9 image-based and 32 coordinate-based fMRI studies) finds a core network of bilateral anterior insula and medial/anterior cingulate for empathy for pain, overlapping with activation during directly experienced pain.

src.l: Claus Lamm, Jean Decety, Tania Singer, 2011, Meta-analytic evidence for common and distinct neural networks associated with directly experienced pain and empathy for pain

s: de Vignemont & Singer (2006) question the assumption, drawn from imaging, that we automatically share others' emotions, and propose that contextual appraisal modulates whether an empathic brain response occurs.

src.l: Frédérique de Vignemont, Tania Singer, 2006, The empathic brain: how, when and why?

s: Zaki (2014) reconciles empathy's reflexive and context-dependent sides by motivation: suffering, material cost and competition push people to avoid empathy; positive affect, affiliation and social desirability push them toward it.

src.l: Jamil Zaki, 2014, Empathy: A motivated account

s: Rizzolatti and colleagues (1999) name 'resonance behaviors' the cases where an individual reproduces, overtly (imitation) or only internally as a neural pattern, an action made by another, and argue the internal kind underlies understanding others' actions.

src.l: Giacomo Rizzolatti, Luciano Fadiga, Leonardo Fogassi, Vittorio Gallese, 1999, Resonance behaviors and mirror neurons

s: In neuroscience the word 'resonance' survives as a name for brain-level sharing (Rizzolatti's 'resonance behaviors', 1999; Singer & Klimecki's 'resonate with' others' feelings, 2014), but in the texts read here it is used as a bare label for matching activity, without the sympathetic-string image that Hume and Lipps spelled out.

src.l: Giacomo Rizzolatti, Luciano Fadiga, Leonardo Fogassi, Vittorio Gallese, 1999, Resonance behaviors and mirror neurons
Tania Singer, Olga M. Klimecki, 2014, Empathy and compassion
Theodor Lipps, 1903, Ästhetik: Psychologie des Schönen und der Kunst, Erster Teil

s: Coplan (2011) argues that the trend to make empathy cover everything from mimicry to high-level perspective taking is the wrong response to its definitional mess, and proposes a narrow concept: imaginative simulation of another's situated psychological states with clear self-other differentiation, distinct from emotional contagion and 'pseudo-empathy'.

src.l: Amy Coplan, 2011, Will the real empathy please stand up? A case for a narrow conceptualization

s: Batson (2009) distinguishes eight related but distinct phenomena that have all been called empathy, answering two different questions (how we know another's state; what moves us to respond with care), from cognitive empathy and posture-matching to projection, perspective taking, personal distress and sympathy.

src.l: C. Daniel Batson, 2009, These things called empathy: eight related but distinct phenomena

s: Cuff et al. (2016) find forty-three distinct definitions of empathy, sort the disagreements into eight themes (cognitive vs affective, congruent vs not, self-other distinction vs merging, automatic vs controlled, etc.), and propose a new composite definition.

src.l: Benjamin M. P. Cuff, Sarah J. Brown, Laura Taylor, Douglas J. Howat, 2016, Empathy: A review of the concept
Benjamin M. P. Cuff, Sarah J. Brown, Laura Taylor, Douglas J. Howat, 2016, Empathy: A review of the concept

s: Cook, Bird, Catmur, Press & Heyes (2014) argue that mirror neurons are forged by domain-general associative learning during development, not evolved as an adaptation for action understanding, so their function must be found by experiment rather than assumed.

src.l: Richard Cook, Geoffrey Bird, Caroline Catmur, Clare Press, Cecilia Heyes, 2014, Mirror neurons: From origin to function

s: Prinz (2011) argues, against what he takes to be Hume's view, that empathy (a vicarious emotion) is not a component, necessary cause, reliable guide, justification or motive of moral judgment, is prone to harmful biases, and that anger, disgust, guilt and admiration are morality's sentimental basis instead.

src.l: Jesse J. Prinz, 2011, Against empathy

s: Hume (Treatise II.1.11) calls the propensity to sympathize the most remarkable quality of human nature: we receive others' inclinations and sentiments 'by communication', even when they differ from or contradict our own.

src.l: David Hume, 1739, A Treatise of Human Nature, vol. 2 (Book II, Of the Passions)
src.loc: Book II, Part I, Sect. XI 'Of the love of fame', p. 73 [scan 77]
src.q: that propenſity we have to ſympathize with others, and to receive by communication their inclinations and ſentiments, however different from, or even contrary to our own.

s: For Hume the mechanism of sympathy is cognitive: an affection is first known by its outward signs as an idea, which is then 'converted into an impression' vivid enough to become the passion itself in the observer.

src.l: David Hume, 1739, A Treatise of Human Nature
src.loc: Book II, Part I, Sect. XI

s: Opening his account of the origin of the natural virtues (Treatise III.3.1), Hume compares sympathy to strings equally wound up: as the motion of one communicates itself to the rest, so affections pass from one person to another and beget corresponding movements in everyone.

src.l: David Hume, 1740, A Treatise of Human Nature, vol. 3 (Book III, Of Morals)
src.loc: Book III, Part III, Sect. I, p. 204 [scan 212]
src.q: As in ſtrings equally wound up, the motion of one communicates itſelf to the reſt ; ſo all the affections readily paſs from one perſon to another, and beget correſpondent movements in every human creature.

s: Hume (Treatise II.2.5) also uses an optical image: the minds of men are mirrors to one another, reflecting each other's emotions, with the 'rays' of passions reverberated and decaying by degrees.

src.l: David Hume, 1739, A Treatise of Human Nature

s: Smith (TMS I.i.1) grounds fellow-feeling in imagination: we come to conceive or be affected by what another feels 'by changing places in fancy with the sufferer', since our senses cannot carry us beyond our own person.

src.l: Adam Smith, 1759, The Theory of Moral Sentiments
src.loc: Part I, Sect. I, ch. 1, p. 3 [scan 15]
src.q: That this is the ſource of our fellow- feeling for the miſery of others, that it is by changing places in fancy with the ſufferer, that we come either to conceive or to be affected by what he feels

s: Smith marks a semantic shift himself: pity and compassion name fellow-feeling with sorrow, while 'sympathy', perhaps originally the same, may now denote fellow-feeling with any passion whatever.

src.l: Adam Smith, 1790, The Theory of Moral Sentiments (sixth edition)

s: Smith's musical image for sympathy is concord, not sounding strings: because the change of situations is only imagined, spectator's and sufferer's feelings 'will never be unisons, they may be concords', which suffices for the harmony of society.

src.l: Adam Smith, 1759, The Theory of Moral Sentiments
src.q: Though they will never be unisons, they may be concords, and this is all that is wanted or required.

s: Smith does not use Hume's image of strings that move one another: a search of the full sixth-edition text of TMS finds no 'string' or 'vibrat-'; his musical vocabulary is of pitch, tone, keeping time, unison and concord, all reached by imagined change of place and deliberate adjustment, not by passive transmission.

src.l: Adam Smith, 1790, The Theory of Moral Sentiments (sixth edition)

s: Vischer (Über das optische Formgefühl, 1873) distinguishes an objective Einfühlung that is indirect: it only subsequently joins the subjective formal functions of sensation (Anempfindung 'for the purpose of Einfühlung') and through them turns, by representation, into the interior of the appearance.

src.l: Robert Vischer, 1873, Über das optische Formgefühl: Ein Beitrag zur Aesthetik
src.q: is indirect in that it only subsequently joins those subjectively formal functions (sensation for the purpose of empathy).
src.qo: ' rekt, als sie nur nachträglich zu jenen subjektiv formalen Funktionen hinzutritt (Anempfindung zum Zweck der Einfühlung).

s: Lipps (Ästhetik I, 1903) uses the sympathetic string explicitly, 'figuratively speaking': every string struck in me tends to set related, similarly tuned strings in me vibrating, as a piano string does in a system of strings; every psychic event awakens the 'Resonanz des Gleichartigen'.

src.l: Theodor Lipps, 1903, Ästhetik: Psychologie des Schönen und der Kunst, Erster Teil

s: Lipps begins his account of the conditions of pleasure (Lustgefühl) with a stretched piano string: any motion can be forced on it, but only the vibration matching its tuning and tension is natural to it.

src.l: Theodor Lipps, 1903, Ästhetik: Psychologie des Schönen und der Kunst, Erster Teil

s: Titchener (1909) introduces 'empathy' as a coinage: feeling or acting gravity, modesty or pride 'in the mind's muscles' is 'a simple case of empathy, if we may coin that term as a rendering of Einfühlung' — a kinaesthetic, not a moral, sense.

src.l: Edward Bradford Titchener, 1909, Lectures on the Experimental Psychology of the Thought-Processes

s: Jahoda (2005) reports that Vischer introduced Einfühlung for art, Lipps extended it to visual illusions and interpersonal understanding and regarded it as basically similar to the old notion of sympathy, while Titchener thought it different and coined 'empathy'; Jahoda concludes Lipps was probably right.

src.l: Gustav Jahoda, 2005, Theodor Lipps and the shift from 'sympathy' to 'empathy'

s: Scheler (Wesen und Formen der Sympathie; 1st ed. 1913) splits fellow-feeling into four distinct facts: immediate feeling-together (Mitfühlen) of one and the same sorrow, fellow-feeling 'about' something (Mitfreude, Mitleid), mere emotional contagion (Gefühlsansteckung), and true identification (Einsfühlung).

src.l: Max Scheler, 1926, Wesen und Formen der Sympathie (3rd ed.; 1st ed. 1913 as Zur Phänomenologie und Theorie der Sympathiegefühle; 2nd ed. 1923)
src.loc: Part A, 'Mitgefühl' (3rd ed. 1926, archive.org djvu text)

s: Scheler holds that emotional contagion has nothing whatever to do with fellow-feeling.

src.l: Max Scheler, 1926, Wesen und Formen der Sympathie (3rd ed.; 1st ed. 1913 as Zur Phänomenologie und Theorie der Sympathiegefühle; 2nd ed. 1923)
src.loc: Part A, section on Gefühlsansteckung (3rd ed. 1926)

s: Scheler argues that understanding another's experience requires neither projective Einfühlung nor imitation, and that where those acts take part they produce not understanding but its possible illusions; elsewhere he names Lipps's projective Einfühlung theory as the target.

src.l: Max Scheler, 1926, Wesen und Formen der Sympathie (3rd ed.; 1st ed. 1913 as Zur Phänomenologie und Theorie der Sympathiegefühle; 2nd ed. 1923)

s: Gallese & Goldman (1998) propose that mirror neurons, which fire both when a monkey acts and when it sees the same action, may let an organism detect others' mental states, as part of or a precursor to simulation-style mind-reading.

src.l: Vittorio Gallese, Alvin Goldman, 1998, Mirror neurons and the simulation theory of mind-reading

s: Rizzolatti & Craighero (2004) review the mirror-neuron mechanism as appearing to play a fundamental role in action understanding and imitation in monkeys and humans.

src.l: Giacomo Rizzolatti, Laila Craighero, 2004, The mirror-neuron system

s: Hickok (2009) argues that no monkey data directly test the theory that mirror neurons are the basis of action understanding, and that human evidence makes a strong case against it.

src.l: Gregory Hickok, 2009, Eight problems for the mirror neuron theory of action understanding in monkeys and humans

s: Singer & Klimecki (2014) define empathy as sharing others' feelings — it 'makes it possible to resonate with' them — while keeping a self-other distinction; without that distinction they call it emotional contagion, and they treat compassion as distinct from empathy.

src.l: Tania Singer, Olga M. Klimecki, 2014, Empathy and compassion

s: Bloom (2017; book form Against Empathy, 2016) argues that empathy, feeling what you think others feel, is narrow, innumerate and biased, can motivate cruelty and burnout, and that compassion is a better guide to moral action.

src.l: Paul Bloom, 2017, Empathy and its discontents

src.l: Joseph Butler, 1726, Fifteen Sermons Preached at the Rolls Chapel
src.loc: Sermon V, 'Upon Compassion', footnote on Hobbes

s: Butler (Sermon V) holds that reason alone is not a sufficient motive of virtue in a creature like man; reason must be joined with the affections God has impressed on the heart, and he rejects the view that a wise man must suppress compassion and all fellow-feeling as a weakness.

src.l: Joseph Butler, 1726, Fifteen Sermons Preached at the Rolls Chapel
Joseph Butler, 1726, Fifteen Sermons Preached at the Rolls Chapel

s: In Sermon I Butler grounds social feeling in a 'natural Principle of Attraction in Man towards Man' and says 'Men are so much one Body' that they feel for each other shame, danger, resentment, honour, prosperity and distress; the image is a social body, not a cosmos.

src.l: Joseph Butler, 1726, Fifteen Sermons Preached at the Rolls Chapel

s: Hutcheson (Essay on the Passions, 1728) names a 'Publick Sense', 'our Determination to be pleased with the Happiness of others, and to be uneasy at their Misery', found in some degree in all men, and identifies it with what some ancients called sensus communis (koinonoemosyne).

src.l: Francis Hutcheson, 1728, An Essay on the Nature and Conduct of the Passions and Affections, with Illustrations on the Moral Sense

s: Against selfish accounts, Hutcheson argues that sympathy is an effect of the constitution of our nature and not chosen for advantage: whatever advantage sympathy with the fortunate may bring, none can be alleged for sympathy with the distressed, and it does not depend on a man's choice whether he is affected.

src.l: Francis Hutcheson, 1728, An Essay on the Nature and Conduct of the Passions and Affections, with Illustrations on the Moral Sense
Francis Hutcheson, 1728, An Essay on the Nature and Conduct of the Passions and Affections, with Illustrations on the Moral Sense

s: Closing the Essay (Treatise I, Sect. VI), Hutcheson says that people should 'be like well-tuned Instruments, affected with every Stroke or Touch upon any one', and points to 'generous Sympathy, Compassion, and Congratulation' as evidence.

src.l: Francis Hutcheson, 1728, An Essay on the Nature and Conduct of the Passions and Affections, with Illustrations on the Moral Sense

s: Rousseau (Second Discourse, Part I) grants man one natural virtue, pitié, a disposition suited to weak beings subject to many ills, more universal and useful because it precedes all use of reflection, and so natural that animals sometimes show signs of it.

src.l: Jean-Jacques Rousseau, 1755, Discours sur l'origine et les fondements de l'inégalité parmi les hommes

s: Rousseau says commiseration is more energetic the more intimately the spectator animal identifies with the suffering animal, that this identification was closer in the state of nature than in the state of reasoning, and that it is reason that engenders amour-propre.

src.l: Jean-Jacques Rousseau, 1755, Discours sur l'origine et les fondements de l'inégalité parmi les hommes

s: Rousseau calls pitié a natural sentiment that, moderating each individual's self-love, contributes to the mutual preservation of the whole species; in the state of nature it 'takes the place of laws, morals and virtue', and against Mandeville he derives generosity, clemency and humanity from it.

src.l: Jean-Jacques Rousseau, 1755, Discours sur l'origine et les fondements de l'inégalité parmi les hommes
Jean-Jacques Rousseau, 1755, Discours sur l'origine et les fondements de l'inégalité parmi les hommes

V = §16) makes compassion, direct participation in another's suffering, the only real basis of voluntary justice and genuine loving-kindness: an action has moral value only so far as it springs from it, and from any other motive none.

src.l: Arthur Schopenhauer, 1903, The Basis of Morality (Preisschrift über die Grundlage der Moral), tr. Arthur Brodrick Bullock
src.loc: Part III, ch. V 'Statement and proof of the only true moral incentive' (German §16)

s: Schopenhauer calls the process by which another's weal and woe go straight to my heart, so that the difference between us is no longer absolute, 'astonishing, indeed hardly comprehensible', 'the great mystery of Ethics, its original phaenomenon', past which only transcendental speculation may step.

src.l: Arthur Schopenhauer, 1903, The Basis of Morality (Preisschrift über die Grundlage der Moral), tr. Arthur Brodrick Bullock

s: In the metaphysical appendix Schopenhauer explains compassion by the unity of being: plurality of individuals is phenomenon, my inmost being subsists in every living thing, a knowledge for which Sanskrit has the formula 'tat tvam asi' and which 'wells up in the shape of Compassion'.

s: Nietzsche (Morgenröthe §133, 'Nicht mehr an sich denken') argues that in what is misleadingly called Mitleid we think strongly, if unconsciously, of ourselves; the pain we feel at another's suffering is our own pain, of which the sufferer is free, so calling it 'Mit-Leid' is misleading.

s: In the Discorsi (1638, First Day) Galileo explains why a plucked lute string sets unstruck strings at the unison, octave and fifth moving by timed pushes of the trembling air, like timed puffs on a pendulum; the Italian passage uses no word for sympathy, and its 'risonanza' names the plucked string's lingering sound, not the answering string.

src.q: Once plucked, the string begins and continues its vibrations for all the time that one hears its resonance last. These vibrations make the air that is near it vibrate and tremble, whose tremors and ripples extend for a great space and go to strike all the strings

s: Herder (Ideen II, 1785) extends the vibrating-body image to persons: the human organization, most homogeneous, is most attuned to echo all other beings; madness can spread 'sympathetically'; children's bodies are a 'lightly resonating string instrument'.

s: Tyndall's Sound (1867) heads the answering-fork experiment 'Sympathetic vibrations' and calls the answering fork a 'sympathetic neighbour', while 'resonant' is reserved for the sounding box; in popular English physics the sympathy word survives into the 1860s.

src.l: John Tyndall, 1867, Sound: A Course of Eight Lectures
src.q: on bringing it close to the silent mounted fork, out of the silence rises a full mellow sound, which is due, not to the fork originally agitated, but to its sympathetic neighbour.

s: Rayleigh's Theory of Sound makes 'resonance' the general term for a forced vibration of a loosely coupled part, and records that the name is 'generally restricted' to the case of nearly equal periods: the answering-string effect becomes a special case of forced vibration.

src.l: Lord Rayleigh (J. W. Strutt), 1894, The Theory of Sound, Vol. I (2nd ed.)
src.q: In the case of approximate equality of periods to which the name of resonance is generally restricted, the amplitude may be very considerable

src.q: The general phenomenon of resonance, though it cannot be exhaustively considered under the head of one degree of freedom, is in the main referable to the same general principles.

s: By 1894 the German edition of Tesla's high-frequency lectures heads a section 'Resonanz' and applies it to electrical oscillations in a capacitor–coil circuit, whose current shifts are 'entirely comparable to the oscillations of a point': the word has left acoustics.

src.q: It is certainly true that we can enlist the aid of resonance for effects at a distance.
src.qo: Es ist wohl wahr, dass wir bei Wirkungen auf Entfernung die Resonanz zu Hilfe nehmen können.

s: On the texts read here, physics moved from sympathy-language to resonance-language in two steps: Galileo (1638) gave the answering string a mechanical cause without the word, while 'sympathy' persisted (Kircher 1673, Holder 1731, Tyndall 1867); German kept Mitschwingen (Helmholtz 1865–77); 'resonance' became the general technical term in Rayleigh's forced-vibration analysis (read in 1894) and spread to electrical circuits (Tesla 1894).

s: On the texts read, 'resonance' in social theory inherits sympathy's job of naming a felt bond between parts, by way of the string image (Herder 1785, Lipps 1903 already use it for persons); Rosa keeps the image but explicitly drops its physical condition of likeness, so his concept borrows the word's vividness while denying the mechanism that gave sympathy and physical resonance their content.
